title: Multi-armed bandits: final test
note: Goal G only (how greedy, ε-greedy and UCB choose). Every item uses a setting the practice doesn't (banner ads, office coffee machines, a study app, podcasts), so the test measures transfer, not recall. Most items make you run a rule on numbers: common sense alone leads to a wrong option. Choice items pair a pick with a reason, all options in the same shape and about the same length, every wrong one a real confusion (some with the right pick for the wrong reason). Number items are typed in (kind number, with a tolerance). type: base = recognise the idea; apply = run the rule on a given state; transfer = a new situation.

items.prompt: A study app estimates how good each lesson format is from how long students stay with it. Format B has been used by 4 students so far, with an estimate of 12 minutes. The fifth student stays 22 minutes. What is the app's estimate for format B now?
items.explain: The estimate is the average of all rewards so far. Four students averaging 12 minutes stayed 48 minutes in all; with the fifth, 48 + 22 = 70 minutes over 5 students, so 14 minutes.

items.prompt: You choose between three office coffee machines with greedy, scoring every cup out of 10. On days 1 to 3 you try each machine once: A scores 4, B 7 and C 6. Day 4's cup scores 3 and day 5's cup scores 5. Which machine do you use on day 6, and why?
options: B: it has given the best single cup so far, the 7
B: greedy stays with the machine that won the trial days
C: its average, 5.5, is now the highest of the three
A: it has had the fewest cups, so it is tried again
items.explain: Day 4 goes to B (best average, 7); its 3 brings B's average to 5. Day 5 goes to C (now the best, 6); its 5 brings C's average to 5.5. On day 6 the averages are A 4, B 5, C 5.5, so greedy uses C. Greedy follows the best average as it changes, not the best single cup or the first winner, and never tries a machine just because it has had few cups.

items.prompt: A podcast app picks between two shows with greedy. Show A is truly the better one: its ratings average 4.5 stars. Show B always gets 3 or 4 stars. To start, each show was recommended once: A happened to get 2 stars and B got 4. Of the next 200 recommendations, how many go to show A?
items.explain: After the first round A's average is 2 and B's is 4. B's ratings are always 3 or 4, so B's average never drops below 3 and always beats A's 2. Greedy never tries A again to find out, so A gets none of the 200: one unlucky first rating hides the better show for good.

items.prompt: The office coffee machines run on greedy. Machine A averages 7.9 over 40 cups, machine B 8.0 over a single cup, and machine C 6.0 over 15 cups. Which machine does greedy pick next, and why?
options: A: greedy trusts the average that rests on the most cups
C: greedy returns to a machine it hasn't used for a while
A or B at random: greedy can't split averages this close
B: greedy compares only the averages, however few cups
items.explain: Greedy picks the highest average, here B's 8.0, and ignores how many cups each average rests on, although one cup says much less than forty. Weighing the number of tries is what UCB adds.

items.prompt: An online shop shows each visitor one of four banner ads, chosen with ε-greedy and ε = 0.2. Banner D has by far the lowest click rate, and the shop has shown it often enough to be sure of that. Of the next 1,000 visitors, about how many are expected to see banner D?
items.explain: D is never the favourite, so it is only shown on explore visits: 20% of visitors, 200 of 1,000. An explore visit picks one of the four banners at random, ignoring what the shop knows, so D gets a quarter of them: 1,000 × 0.2 ÷ 4 = 50.

items.prompt: Two shops run the same five banner ads for a year with ε-greedy, one with ε = 0.02 and the other with ε = 0.5. What does each risk?
options: ε = 0.02 shows known-worse banners to many visitors; ε = 0.5 risks staying on a worse banner
ε = 0.02 risks staying on a worse banner; ε = 0.5 shows known-worse banners to many visitors
Neither risks anything: both find the best banner, ε only sets how fast the averages settle
Only ε = 0.02 risks anything: exploring more always brings in more clicks over a whole year
items.explain: With ε = 0.02 the shop hardly explores, so an unlucky start can keep it on a worse banner for a long time (too little exploration). With ε = 0.5 half the visitors get a random banner, including ones the shop already knows are worse (too much exploration).

items.prompt: A podcast app recommends shows with ε-greedy, ε = 0.1. Show A averages 4.6 stars over 300 plays, show B 2.1 over 300 plays, and show C 3.9 over only 3 plays. On the explore rounds, which show is picked most often?
options: None of them: an explore pick is random, so each show is equally likely
C: explore rounds go to the show with the fewest plays, to learn about it
A: explore rounds still lean towards the show with the best average
B or C: exploring means leaving the favourite for one of the others
items.explain: On an explore round ε-greedy picks any show at random: it looks neither at the averages nor at how often each show was played. So A, B and C each get a third of the explore rounds, even B, which is known to be poor. Going to the least-played show is closer to what UCB does.

items.prompt: A study app picks quiz formats with UCB1. It is round t = 50 (ln 50 ≈ 3.91). Format B has been used n = 8 times, and its average score so far is 0.60. What is format B's UCB score?
The office coffee machines now run on UCB1. It is day t = 20 (ln 20 ≈ 3.0). Machine A averages 7.0 over 10 cups, B 6.0 over 2 cups, and C 6.6 over 8 cups. Which machine does UCB pick, and why?
options: B: with only 2 cups it gets by far the biggest bonus, and that decides
A: once every machine has been tried, UCB goes with the best average
Any of them: UCB picks a machine at random on a share of the days
A: its average plus its bonus, about 7.77, is the highest of the three
items.explain: Scores = average + √(2 ln t / n): A = 7.0 + √(6/10) ≈ 7.77, B = 6.0 + √(6/2) ≈ 7.73, C = 6.6 + √(6/8) ≈ 7.47. B has the biggest bonus, but A's higher average wins by a little. UCB always adds the bonus, it never picks at random, and it doesn't drop the bonus once everything has been tried.

items.prompt: A podcast app recommends shows with UCB1; take ln t ≈ 4.6 on the next two rounds. Show A averages 4.0 stars over 50 plays, show C 3.0 over 4 plays. C is recommended next and gets 3 stars. Which show is recommended on the round after that, and why?
options: C: it keeps its large bonus until its plays catch up with A's
A: one more play shrinks C's bonus, and C's score drops below A's
A: C's rating of 3 stars pulled C's average down below A's score
C: a show that was just recommended is recommended again until it falls
items.explain: Before: A = 4.0 + √(9.2/50) ≈ 4.43, C = 3.0 + √(9.2/4) ≈ 4.52, so C is picked. Its new 3 stars leave C's average at 3.0, but n goes from 4 to 5, so its bonus shrinks to √(9.2/5) ≈ 1.36 and its score to 4.36, below A's 4.43. Every play shrinks a show's bonus; UCB moves on as soon as another score is higher.
